Often he anticipated their wrongs and wishes. He encouraged them that their society should be as frank in conversation as he was generous in contributions. But the instant they ceased to be authors, artists, or philosophers, and their communications arose from anything but the intellectual quality which had originally interested him, he saw them no more.

Jews are intellectual. Hegel would say that without culture there can be no great ideas. Ideas emerge from community, from culture, from belonging. If you think you are intellectually superior to culture, nation, people, you will not produce great ideas.

Not merely in these unquestionable shapes did his notice command intellect. There was not an adventurer in Europe with whom he was not familiar. No minister of state has such communication as Sidonia. He held relations with all the clever outcasts of the world: Greeks, Armenians, Moors, secret Jews, Tartars, Gypsies.

Jews are international and cosmopolitan first and foremost. Over time, in contact with so many different groups, he came to believe that the superior race, the greatest race of humanity, are the Jews because they refuse to intermarry or breed with other cultures. This is ironic, as the Nazis would later use this idea to justify the Holocaust.

In this country, says Addison, since the peace there has been an attempt to advocate a reconstruction of society on a purely rational basis. The principle of utility has been powerfully developed. I speak not lightly of the labors of those disciples. I bow to intellect in every form and we should be grateful to any school of philosophers even if we disagree with them.

Attempts to reconstruct society on a basis of material motives and calculations have failed. It must ultimately fail under any circumstances, especially in an ancient and densely populated kingdom. How limited is human reason? The profoundest inquiries are most conscious. We are not indebted to the reason of man for any of the great achievements which are landmarks of human action and progress.

It was not reason that besieged Troy; it was not reason that sent forth Saracens from the desert to conquer the world. Reason did not inspire the crusades or institute monastic orders, nor produce the Jesuits or create the French Revolution. Men are truly great when they act from passion, never irresistible but when they appeal to imagination. Even Mormons count more votaries than Bentham.

So Sono emphasizes the limitations of British philosophy, prioritizing imagination over reason in governance and society.
